title: LA BARBE BLEÜE
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
source: Charles Perrault, « LA BARBE BLEÜE », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: Bluebeard is the tale of a rich man whose blue beard frightens every woman, of the young wife handed every key in the house and forbidden one small room, and of the sister who keeps watch from the tower. Perrault sets it in a grand household of his own day, with storerooms of furnishings, full-length mirrors and a hidden back stair, and tells it briskly, without softening what lies behind the closet door; the notes gloss those rooms and customs, and the words whose sense has moved since 1697. Two verse morals close it: the first chides curiosity, and the second teases that husbands so fearsome belong to a tale of times past.

glossary.fée: fée — enchanted, having fairy power (adjective use: «la clef estoit Fée», the key was enchanted); as a noun, fairy (f.)

sentences.t: Il estoit une fois un homme qui avoit de belles maisons à la Ville & à la Campagne, de la vaisselle d’or & d’argent, des meubles en broderie, & des carosses tout dorez ;
sentences.say: Il était une fois un homme qui avait de belles maisons à la Ville et à la Campagne, de la vaisselle d’or et d’argent, des meubles en broderie, et des carrosses tout dorez ;
sentences.l: There was one time a man who had fine houses in the Town and in the Country, plate of gold and of silver, furniture in embroidery, and coaches all gilded;
sentences.i: Once upon a time there was a man who had fine houses in town and in the country, gold and silver plate, embroidered furnishings, and coaches gilded all over;
sentences.n: «Il estoit une fois» is the storyteller’s fixed opening: «il» is the impersonal ‘it’, standing where English says ‘there’, «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était» ‘was’, and «une fois» is ‘one time, once’. Lectorium gives it the matching English formula, ‘once upon a time’, in every tale it opens (Cendrillon prints it «Il eſtoit», with the long s). «avoit» is likewise «avait» ‘had’. «vaisselle d’or & d’argent» is plate, the table vessels of gold and silver that displayed a great household’s wealth. «meubles» covered more than chairs and tables: the hangings, bed-curtains and upholstery of a room, here worked in embroidery. «carosses» is «carrosses» ‘coaches’, and «dorez» is «dorés» ‘gilded’, a participle in «-ez». «&» is the printer’s sign for «et» ‘and’, and the capitals on «Ville» and «Campagne» are the printer’s too.

sentences.t: mais par malheur cet homme avoit la Barbe-bleüe : cela le rendoit si laid & si terrible, qu’il n’estoit ni femme ni fille qui ne s’enfuit de devant luy.
sentences.say: mais par malheur cet homme avait la Barbe-bleue : cela le rendait si laid et si terrible, qu’il n’était ni femme ni fille qui ne s’enfuit de devant lui.
sentences.l: but by ill luck this man had the Blue Beard: that made him so ugly and so terrible, that there was neither woman nor girl who did not flee from before him.
sentences.i: but, as ill luck would have it, this man had a blue beard, and it made him so ugly and so fearsome that there was not a woman or a girl who did not run from the sight of him.
sentences.n: «la Barbe-bleüe» is at first a description, ‘a blue beard’, though the printer’s capitals already make it look like a name, and so it becomes: «la Barbe bleuë», spelt several ways in this book, is ‘Blue Beard’ in the literal line and ‘Bluebeard’ in the idiomatic one. «barbe» ‘beard’ is feminine, hence «la», even though it names a man. «rendoit» is «rendait» ‘made’, and «terrible» is ‘fearsome, dreadful’, stronger than the word has become. «il n’estoit ni femme ni fille» ‘there was neither woman nor girl’ uses «être» for ‘there was’, as literary French still can. «s’enfuit» is best read as the imperfect subjunctive (modern «s’enfuît»), which a relative clause after a negative calls for; it is a formal tense that modern speech avoids, and English renders it with a plain past. Without its accent it is spelt like the passé simple «s’enfuit» ‘fled’. «luy» is «lui» ‘him’, with the 1697 y.

sentences.t: Une de ses Voisines, Dame de qualité, avoit deux filles parfaitement belles.
sentences.say: Une de ses Voisines, Dame de qualité, avait deux filles parfaitement belles.
sentences.l: One of his Neighbours, a Lady of quality, had two daughters perfectly beautiful.
sentences.i: One of his neighbours, a lady of rank, had two daughters of perfect beauty.
sentences.n: «Dame de qualité» is a lady of rank: «de qualité» in 1697 meant ‘of good birth, of the nobility’, not ‘of good quality’. «filles» is both ‘girls’ and ‘daughters’. The printer capitalises «Voisines» and «Dame» as he does many common nouns.

sentences.t: Il luy en demanda une en Mariage, en luy laissa le choix de celle qu’elle voudroit luy donner.
sentences.say: Il lui en demanda une en Mariage, en lui laissa le choix de celle qu’elle voudrait lui donner.
sentences.l: He asked her for one of them in Marriage, [and] left her the choice of the one that she would wish to give him.
sentences.i: He asked her for one of them in marriage, and left it to her to choose which one she would give him.
sentences.n: «demanda» ‘asked’ is the passé simple, the tense in which French tells a story: each verb in it is an event, done and finished. It has left everyday speech, where the passé composé («il a demandé») took its place, and English renders it with its plain past. In «Il luy en demanda une» ‘he to her of them asked one’ the pronouns stand before the verb, «en» meaning ‘of them’. The witness prints «en luy laissa», which does not construe; the sense requires «et luy laissa» ‘and left her’, the literal line supplies ‘and’ in brackets, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «voudroit» is «voudrait» ‘would wish’.

sentences.t: Elles n’en vouloient point toutes deux, & se le renvoyoient l’une à l’autre, ne pouvant se resoudre à prendre un homme qui eut la barbe bleüe.
sentences.say: Elles n’en voulaient point toutes deux, et se le renvoyaient l’une à l’autre, ne pouvant se résoudre à prendre un homme qui eut la barbe bleue.
sentences.l: They wanted none of him, both of them, and sent him back the one to the other, not being able to resolve themselves to take a man who had the blue beard.
sentences.i: Neither of them would have him, and each kept passing him on to the other, for neither could bring herself to take a man with a blue beard.
sentences.n: «n’en vouloient point» ‘wanted none of him’: «en» stands for the suitor, as in «ne vouloir point de quelqu’un» ‘to want none of someone’, «ne … point» is a firm ‘not’, and «vouloient» is the 1697 spelling of «voulaient», an «oi» where modern French writes «ai». «toutes deux» is ‘both’. «se le renvoyoient l’une à l’autre» ‘sent him back to each other, the one to the other’: the imperfect makes it a game that went on. «se resoudre à» (modern «se résoudre») is ‘to bring oneself to’. «eut» stands for «eût», the imperfect subjunctive again, for the kind of man they could not take; here the beard is a plain description, in lower case.

sentences.t: Ce qui les degoûtoit encore, c’est qu’il avoit déja épousé plusieurs femmes, & qu’on ne sçavoit ce que ces femmes estoient devenuës.
sentences.say: Ce qui les dégoûtait encore, c’est qu’il avait déjà épousé plusieurs femmes, et qu’on ne savait ce que ces femmes étaient devenues.
sentences.l: What put them off still more, it is that he had already married several wives, and that one did not know what those wives had become.
sentences.i: What set them against him still more was that he had already married several wives, and no one knew what had become of them.
sentences.n: «Ce qui … c’est que» ‘what … it is that’ is the French way of putting weight on what follows. «degoûtoit» (modern «dégoûtait») is ‘put off, turned against’, milder here than ‘disgusted’. «femmes» serves for ‘women’ and ‘wives’ alike. «on ne sçavoit» ‘one did not know’: «sçavoit» is the 1697 spelling of «savait», and «ne» stands alone, as it often does with this verb. «estoient devenuës» ‘had become’: «devenir» forms its compound tenses with «être», and «devenuës» (modern «devenues») agrees with «femmes». «déja» lacks the grave accent of modern «déjà».

sentences.t: La Barbe bleuë pour faire connoissance, les mena avec leur mere, & trois ou quatre de leurs meilleures amies, & quelques jeunes gens du voisinage, à une de ses maisons de Campagne, où on demeura huit jours entiers.
sentences.say: La Barbe bleue pour faire connaissance, les mena avec leur mère, et trois ou quatre de leurs meilleures amies, et quelques jeunes gens du voisinage, à une de ses maisons de Campagne, où on demeura huit jours entiers.
sentences.l: Blue Beard, to make acquaintance, took them with their mother, and three or four of their best friends, and some young people of the neighbourhood, to one of his houses in the Country, where they stayed eight whole days.
sentences.i: To become better acquainted, Bluebeard took them, with their mother, three or four of their closest friends and some young people of the neighbourhood, to one of his country houses, where they all stayed a full week.
sentences.n: From here «la Barbe bleuë» is his name: ‘Blue Beard’, ‘Bluebeard’, with the feminine «la» of «barbe». «connoissance» is «connaissance» ‘acquaintance’, the 1697 «oi» again. «mena» is the passé simple of «mener» ‘to take, lead’. «on» ‘one’ takes in the whole party. «huit jours» ‘eight days’ is the ordinary French way of saying ‘a week’, counting the first day and the last, and the idiomatic line says ‘a week’.

sentences.t: Ce n’estoit que promenades, que parties de chasse & de pesche, que danses & festins, que collations : on ne dormoit point, & on passoit toute la nuit à se faire des malices les uns aux autres :
sentences.say: Ce n’était que promenades, que parties de chasse et de pêche, que danses et festins, que collations : on ne dormait point, et on passait toute la nuit à se faire des malices les uns aux autres :
sentences.l: It was nothing but walks, but parties of hunting and of fishing, but dances and feasts, but collations: one did not sleep at all, and one passed the whole night in playing tricks on one another:
sentences.i: There was nothing but strolling, hunting and fishing parties, dancing and feasting and light suppers; nobody slept, and they spent the whole night playing pranks on one another;
sentences.n: «Ce n’estoit que …, que …» ‘it was only …, only …’: «ne … que» is ‘nothing but’, and repeating «que» before each pleasure piles them up. «pesche» is «pêche» ‘fishing’, with the 1697 s before a consonant where modern French has a circumflex. A «collation» was a light meal of fruit, sweets and cold dishes, served between the main meals or late in the evening. «se faire des malices» ‘to do one another mischiefs’ is to play tricks. The imperfects («estoit», «dormoit», «passoit») describe how the days and nights went, one after another.

sentences.t: enfin tout alla si bien, que la cadette commença à trouver que le Maistre du logis n’avoit plus la barbe si bleüe, & que c’estoit un fort honneste homme.
sentences.say: enfin tout alla si bien, que la cadette commença à trouver que le Maître du logis n’avait plus la barbe si bleue, et que c’était un fort honnête homme.
sentences.l: in short all went so well, that the younger began to find that the Master of the house no longer had the beard so blue, and that he was a very worthy man.
sentences.i: in the end it all went so well that the younger sister began to think the beard of the master of the house was not so very blue after all, and that he was a true gentleman.
sentences.n: «enfin» is ‘in short, in the end’, and «alla», «commença» are passé simple. «la cadette» is ‘the younger (daughter)’. «Maistre du logis» is «maître du logis» ‘master of the house’. «fort» is ‘very’, and «un fort honneste homme» is more than ‘a very honest man’: the «honnête homme» was the ideal of polite society in Perrault’s day, a man of good breeding, courteous, agreeable and at ease in company. The literal line says ‘worthy’ and the idiomatic ‘gentleman’; the same words return at the tale’s end.

sentences.t: Dés qu’on fust de retour à la Ville, le Mariage se conclut.
sentences.say: Dès qu’on fût de retour à la Ville, le Mariage se conclut.
sentences.l: As soon as they were back in the Town, the Marriage was concluded.
sentences.i: As soon as they were back in town, the marriage was settled.
sentences.n: «Dés» is «dès» ‘from, as soon as’. «fust» is printed with an s, the spelling the book otherwise keeps for the imperfect subjunctive «fût»; after «dès que» the sense needs the passé simple «fut» ‘was’, which the book elsewhere prints without the s («dés qu’on fut sorti de table» in the Sleeping Beauty). The two sound alike. «se conclut» ‘concluded itself’ is the French reflexive standing for a passive, ‘was concluded’. «on» is ‘one’, the whole party, and English says ‘they’.

sentences.t: Au bout d’un mois, la Barbe bleüe dit à sa femme qu’il estoit obligé de faire un voyage en Province, de six semaines au moins, pour une affaire de consequence ;
sentences.say: Au bout d’un mois, la Barbe bleue dit à sa femme qu’il était obligé de faire un voyage en Province, de six semaines au moins, pour une affaire de conséquence ;
sentences.l: At the end of a month, Blue Beard said to his wife that he was obliged to make a journey into the Provinces, of six weeks at least, for a matter of consequence;
sentences.i: After a month, Bluebeard told his wife that he was obliged to go on a journey into the provinces, for six weeks at least, on a matter of importance;
sentences.n: «en Province» ‘into the Province’: to a Parisian, the whole of France outside the capital. «affaire de consequence» is a matter of importance; «consequence» lacks the accent of modern «conséquence». The reported speech that begins here with «qu’il estoit obligé» runs on through the next unit, each wish hanging on «que» ‘that’, until he breaks into his own words. «dit» ‘said’ is passé simple, spelt like the present.

sentences.t: qu’il la prioit de se bien divertir pendant son absence, qu’elle fit venir ses bonnes amies, qu’elle les menast à la Campagne si elle vouloit, que par tout elle fit bonne chere :
sentences.say: qu’il la priait de se bien divertir pendant son absence, qu’elle fit venir ses bonnes amies, qu’elle les menât à la Campagne si elle voulait, que par tout elle fit bonne chère :
sentences.l: that he begged her to amuse herself well during his absence, that she should have her good friends come, that she should take them to the Country if she wished, that everywhere she should make good cheer:
sentences.i: that he begged her to enjoy herself while he was away: she should invite her close friends, take them to the country if she liked, and keep a good table wherever she was.
sentences.n: «prioit» (modern «priait») is ‘begged, asked’. «se bien divertir» sets «bien» before the verb, where modern French says «bien se divertir». «fit venir» ‘should make come’ is to send for her friends, to have them come: «fit» (modern «fît») and «menast» (modern «menât») are imperfect subjunctives, the form a reported wish takes after «que», and English says ‘should’. «faire bonne chère» ‘to make good cheer’ is to eat well and entertain freely: «chère» first meant ‘face’, then the welcome shown on it, then the fare set before a guest. «par tout» is «partout» ‘everywhere’.

sentences.t: Voilà, luy dit-il, les clefs des deux grands gardemeubles, voilà celles de la vaisselle d’or & d’argent qui ne sert pas tous les jours, voilà celles de mes coffres forts, où est mon or & mon argent, celles des cassettes où sont mes pierreries, et voilà le passe par tout de tous les appartemens :
sentences.say: Voilà, lui dit-il, les clefs des deux grands garde-meubles, voilà celles de la vaisselle d’or et d’argent qui ne sert pas tous les jours, voilà celles de mes coffres forts, où est mon or et mon argent, celles des cassettes où sont mes pierreries, et voilà le passe par tout de tous les appartements :
sentences.l: Here are, he said to her, the keys of the two great furniture-stores, here are those of the plate of gold and of silver that does not serve every day, here are those of my strong-boxes, where is my gold and my silver, those of the caskets where are my jewels, and here is the pass-everywhere of all the apartments:
sentences.i: Here, he said, are the keys to the two great storerooms of furniture; here are the keys to the gold and silver plate that is not in everyday use; here are those to my strongboxes, where my gold and silver are kept, and those to the caskets that hold my jewels; and here is the master key to every apartment in the house.
sentences.n: The book prints no quotation marks: speech is marked only by tags such as «luy dit-il» ‘he said to her’, and here the husband’s reported words turn into his own. «Voilà» ‘see there’ is ‘here is, here are’. A «gardemeuble» (modern «garde-meuble») was a storeroom for the furnishings of a great house: tapestries, hangings, beds and chairs, changed with the seasons or brought out for occasions. «coffres forts» are strongboxes, «cassettes» small caskets, and «pierreries» precious stones. «le passe par tout» (modern «passe-partout», ‘pass everywhere’) is a master key. An «appartement» was a suite of rooms in a great house; «appartemens» drops the t of modern «appartements».

sentences.t: pour cette petite clef-cy, c’est la clef du cabinet au bout de la grande gallerie de l’appartement bas :
sentences.say: pour cette petite clef-ci, c’est la clef du cabinet au bout de la grande galerie de l’appartement bas :
sentences.l: as for this little key here, it is the key of the closet at the end of the great gallery of the lower apartment:
sentences.i: As for this little key, it is the key to the closet at the end of the long gallery on the ground floor.
sentences.n: A «cabinet» here is a small private room, a closet, the most retired room of a suite, where a person of rank kept papers and treasures; later in the tale, among the furnishings in the storerooms upstairs, the same word names a piece of furniture. «clef-cy» is «clef-ci» ‘this key here’, with the 1697 y. «gallerie» is «galerie», a long room for walking and display. «l’appartement bas» ‘the low suite’ is the one on the ground floor.

sentences.t: ouvrez tout, allez par tout, mais pour ce petit cabinet je vous deffens d’y entrer, & je vous le deffens de telle sorte, que s’il vous arrive de l’ouvrir, il n’y a rien que vous ne deviez attendre de ma colere.
sentences.say: ouvrez tout, allez par tout, mais pour ce petit cabinet je vous défends d’y entrer, et je vous le défends de telle sorte, que s’il vous arrive de l’ouvrir, il n’y a rien que vous ne deviez attendre de ma colère.
sentences.l: open everything, go everywhere, but as for this little closet I forbid you to enter there, and I forbid it to you in such a manner, that if it happens to you to open it, there is nothing that you should not expect from my anger.
sentences.i: Open everything, go everywhere; but that little closet I forbid you to enter, and I forbid it so strictly that, should you happen to open it, there is nothing you may not expect from my anger.
sentences.n: «deffens» is the 1697 spelling of «défends», from «défendre» ‘to forbid’. «s’il vous arrive de» ‘if it happens to you to’ is ‘if you should happen to’. «il n’y a rien que vous ne deviez attendre» ‘there is nothing that you must not expect’: after a negative, the «que» clause takes the subjunctive «deviez» with its own «ne», and the double negative means that anything at all may be expected. «colere» is «colère». He says «vous» to his wife, as husbands and wives of rank commonly did; the English stays ‘you’.

sentences.t: Elle promit d’observer exactement tout ce qui luy venoist d’estre ordonné :
sentences.say: Elle promit d’observer exactement tout ce qui lui venait d’être ordonné :
sentences.l: She promised to observe exactly all that had just been ordered her:
sentences.i: She promised to observe to the letter all that she had just been told;
sentences.n: «venir de» with an infinitive is ‘to have just (done)’, so «qui luy venoit d’estre ordonné» is ‘which had just been ordered her’. The witness prints «venoist», with an s that the imperfect «venoit» does not have; it may be a slip of the printer or of the transcription, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «estre» is «être»; «promit» is passé simple.

sentences.t: & luy, aprés l’avoir embrassée, il monte dans son carosse, & part pour son voyage.
sentences.say: et lui, après l’avoir embrassée, il monte dans son carrosse, et part pour son voyage.
sentences.l: and he, after having embraced her, he gets into his coach, and leaves for his journey.
sentences.i: and he, having taken her in his arms, climbed into his coach and set off on his journey.
sentences.n: «luy», the stressed form «lui», sets ‘he’ apart before «il» repeats it. The telling drops into the present («monte», «part») for the quick departure; the idiomatic line keeps the past. «embrasser», built on «bras» ‘arm’, is ‘to take in one’s arms’. «aprés» carries the acute accent where modern «après» has a grave.

sentences.t: Les voisines & les bonnes amies n’attendirent pas qu’on les envoyast querir pour aller chez la jeune Mariée, tant elles avoient d’impatience de voir toutes les richesses de sa Maison, n’ayant osé y venir pendant que le Mari y estoit, à cause de sa Barbe bleuë qui leur faisoit peur.
sentences.say: Les voisines et les bonnes amies n’attendirent pas qu’on les envoyât quérir pour aller chez la jeune Mariée, tant elles avaient d’impatience de voir toutes les richesses de sa Maison, n’ayant osé y venir pendant que le Mari y était, à cause de sa Barbe bleue qui leur faisait peur.
sentences.l: The neighbours and the good friends did not wait for someone to send to fetch them to go to the young Bride’s house, so much impatience they had to see all the riches of her House, not having dared to come there while the Husband was there, because of his Blue Beard that made them afraid.
sentences.i: The neighbours and close friends did not wait to be sent for before calling on the young bride, so impatient were they to see all the riches of her house; they had not dared to come while her husband was there, because of his blue beard, which frightened them.
sentences.n: «envoyer querir» ‘to send to fetch’ is ‘to send for’; «envoyast» (modern «envoyât») is the imperfect subjunctive that «attendre que» ‘to wait until’ calls for, and «attendirent» is passé simple. «chez» is ‘at the house of’, which the literal line spells out. «tant elles avoient d’impatience» ‘so much impatience did they have’. «n’ayant osé» has «ne» alone, as often with «oser» ‘to dare’. «sa Barbe bleuë» is the beard itself this time, not the name; «sa» agrees with «barbe» and means ‘his’.

sentences.t: Les voilà aussi-tost à parcourir les chambres, les cabinets, les garderobes, toutes plus belles & plus riches les unes que les autres.
sentences.say: Les voilà aussitôt à parcourir les chambres, les cabinets, les garde-robes, toutes plus belles et plus riches les unes que les autres.
sentences.l: There they are at once going through the rooms, the closets, the wardrobes, all more beautiful and more rich the ones than the others.
sentences.i: At once they were off through the bedchambers, the closets and the dressing rooms, each finer and richer than the last.
sentences.n: «Les voilà à» with an infinitive, ‘there they are at’, sets the scene in motion. «aussi-tost» is «aussitôt» ‘at once’. A «garderobe» (modern «garde-robe») was a small room beside a bedchamber, where clothes were kept. «toutes plus belles … les unes que les autres» ‘all more beautiful the ones than the others’ is the French idiom for ‘each finer than the next’; «toutes» is feminine, agreeing with the nearest noun, «garderobes», even though «cabinets» between them is masculine.

sentences.t: Elles monterent en suite aux gardemeubles, où elles ne pouvoient assez admirer le nombre & la beauté des tapisseries, des lits, des sophas, des cabinets, des gueridons, des tables & des miroirs, où l’on se voyoit depuis les pieds jusqu’à la teste, & dont les bordures les unes de glace, les autres d’argent, & de vermeil doré, estoient les plus belles & les plus magnifiques qu’on eut jamais veuës :
sentences.say: Elles montèrent en suite aux garde-meubles, où elles ne pouvaient assez admirer le nombre et la beauté des tapisseries, des lits, des sofas, des cabinets, des guéridons, des tables et des miroirs, où l’on se voyait depuis les pieds jusqu’à la tête, et dont les bordures les unes de glace, les autres d’argent, et de vermeil doré, étaient les plus belles et les plus magnifiques qu’on eut jamais vues :
sentences.l: They went up next to the furniture-stores, where they could not enough admire the number and the beauty of the tapestries, of the beds, of the sofas, of the cabinets, of the stands, of the tables and of the mirrors, where one saw oneself from the feet up to the head, and of which the frames, some of glass, the others of silver, and of gilded silver, were the most beautiful and the most magnificent that one had ever seen:
sentences.i: Next they went up to the storerooms, where they could not admire enough the number and beauty of the tapestries, beds, sofas, cabinets, candlestands, tables and mirrors, in which one could see oneself from head to foot, and whose frames, some of glass, others of silver and silver-gilt, were the finest and most magnificent ever seen.
sentences.n: «monterent» is «montèrent», passé simple, and «en suite» is «ensuite» ‘next’. «cabinets» here are pieces of furniture, cabinets with drawers and doors, often richly inlaid; «gueridons» (modern «guéridons») were small pedestal stands for a candlestick. Mirrors that showed a person from head to foot were among the costliest luxuries of the age, since large panes of glass were hard to make. «vermeil doré» is silver-gilt, and frames «de glace» are of mirror glass. «teste» is «tête», «eut» stands for «eût», and «veuës» for «vues» ‘seen’.

sentences.t: Elles ne cessoient d’exagerer & d’envier le bonheur de leur amie, qui cependant ne se divertissoit point à voir toutes ces richesses, à cause de l’impatience qu’elle avoit d’aller ouvrir le cabinet de l’appartement bas.
sentences.say: Elles ne cessaient d’exagérer et d’envier le bonheur de leur amie, qui cependant ne se divertissait point à voir toutes ces richesses, à cause de l’impatience qu’elle avait d’aller ouvrir le cabinet de l’appartement bas.
sentences.l: They did not cease to extol and to envy the good fortune of their friend, who meanwhile took no amusement at all in seeing all these riches, because of the impatience that she had to go open the closet of the lower apartment.
sentences.i: They could not stop praising and envying the good fortune of their friend, who all the while took no pleasure in seeing all these riches, so impatient was she to go and open the closet on the ground floor.
sentences.n: «exagerer» (modern «exagérer») in 1697 meant to enlarge on something in words, to make much of it; here it is admiring talk, and the English gives it as praise, though the sense of saying more than the truth was already part of the word. «bonheur» here is ‘good fortune’. «cependant» has its older sense ‘meanwhile, all the while’. «se divertir à» is ‘to take pleasure in’.

sentences.t: Elle fut si pressée de sa curiosité, que sans considerer qu’il estoit malhonneste de quitter sa compagnie, elle y descendit par un petit escalier dérobé, & avec tant de precipitation, qu’elle pensa se rompre le cou deux ou trois fois.
sentences.say: Elle fut si pressée de sa curiosité, que sans considérer qu’il était malhonnête de quitter sa compagnie, elle y descendit par un petit escalier dérobé, et avec tant de précipitation, qu’elle pensa se rompre le cou deux ou trois fois.
sentences.l: She was so pressed by her curiosity, that without considering that it was ill-mannered to leave her company, she went down there by a little hidden staircase, and with such haste, that she came near to breaking her neck two or three times.
sentences.i: She was so driven by her curiosity that, without stopping to think how rude it was to leave her guests, she went down by a little hidden staircase, and in such haste that two or three times she all but broke her neck.
sentences.n: «malhonneste» (modern «malhonnête») meant ‘impolite, ill-mannered’, the opposite of the «honneste homme»’s good manners, not ‘dishonest’. «sa compagnie» is the company she was entertaining. An «escalier dérobé» ‘stolen staircase’ is a concealed back stair, of the kind great houses had for servants and for private comings and goings. «penser» with an infinitive, here in the passé simple «pensa», is ‘to come near to (doing)’. «precipitation» is ‘haste’.

sentences.t: Estant arrivée à la porte du cabinet, elle s’y arresta quelque temps, songeant à la deffense que son Mari luy avoit faite, & considerant qu’il pourroit luy arriver malheur d’avoir esté desobéïssante ;
sentences.say: Étant arrivée à la porte du cabinet, elle s’y arrêta quelque temps, songeant à la défense que son Mari lui avait faite, et considérant qu’il pourrait lui arriver malheur d’avoir été désobéissante ;
sentences.l: Being arrived at the door of the closet, she stopped there some time, thinking of the prohibition that her Husband had laid on her, and considering that misfortune could befall her for having been disobedient;
sentences.i: When she reached the door of the closet she stood there a while, thinking of what her husband had forbidden her, and reflecting that harm might come to her for having disobeyed;
sentences.n: «Estant arrivée» ‘being arrived’: «arriver» forms its perfect with «estre» (modern «être», participle «estant»), and «arrivée» agrees with the wife. «s’arrester» is «s’arrêter» ‘to stop’. «deffense» (modern «défense») is the prohibition he laid on her, from «deffendre» ‘to forbid’. «il pourroit luy arriver malheur» ‘there could happen to her misfortune’ has the impersonal «il», and «pourroit» is «pourrait». «desobéïssante» is «désobéissante», printed with a diaeresis that keeps the «i» a separate vowel.

sentences.t: mais la tentation estoit si forte qu’elle ne put la surmonter :
sentences.say: mais la tentation était si forte qu’elle ne put la surmonter :
sentences.l: but the temptation was so strong that she could not overcome it:
sentences.n: «put» is the passé simple of «pouvoir» ‘could’. «la» stands for «la tentation» and sits before the infinitive «surmonter» ‘to overcome’.

sentences.t: elle prit donc la petite clef, & ouvrit en tremblant la porte du cabinet.
sentences.say: elle prit donc la petite clef, et ouvrit en tremblant la porte du cabinet.
sentences.l: she took therefore the little key, and opened trembling the door of the closet.
sentences.i: so she took the little key and, trembling, opened the door of the closet.
sentences.n: «en tremblant» ‘in trembling’ is the gerund, telling how she opened it, set between the verb and its object. «prit» and «ouvrit» are passé simple, and «donc» is ‘so, therefore’.

sentences.t: D’abord elle ne vit rien, parce que les fenestres estoient fermées ;
sentences.say: D’abord elle ne vit rien, parce que les fenêtres étaient fermées ;
sentences.l: At first she saw nothing, because the windows were closed;
sentences.i: At first she could see nothing, for the windows were shut;
sentences.n: «fenestres» is «fenêtres» ‘windows’, the 1697 s before a consonant again. «vit» is the passé simple of «voir» ‘to see’. «D’abord» is ‘at first’.

sentences.t: aprés quelques momens elle commença à voir que le plancher estoit tout couvert de sang caillé, dans lequel se miroient les corps de plusieurs femmes mortes, & attachées le long des murs.
sentences.say: après quelques moments elle commença à voir que le plancher était tout couvert de sang caillé, dans lequel se miraient les corps de plusieurs femmes mortes, et attachées le long des murs.
sentences.l: after some moments she began to see that the floor was all covered with clotted blood, in which were mirrored the bodies of several women dead, and fastened along the walls.
sentences.i: after a few moments she began to make out that the floor was covered all over with clotted blood, and that in it were reflected the bodies of several dead women, fastened along the walls.
sentences.n: «sang caillé» is ‘clotted blood’, and «plancher» ‘floor’. «se miroient» (modern «se miraient») ‘mirrored themselves’: the bodies were reflected in the blood as in a glass, with the verb of the same family as the «miroirs» admired upstairs. «attachées le long des murs» ‘fastened along the walls’: the French does not say how, and neither does the English. «momens» drops the t of modern «moments».

sentences.t: (C’estoit toutes les femmes que la Barbe bleuë avoit épousées & qu’il avoit égorgées l’une aprés l’autre.)
sentences.say: (C’était toutes les femmes que la Barbe bleue avait épousées et qu’il avait égorgées l’une après l’autre.)
sentences.l: (It was all the wives that Blue Beard had married and whose throats he had cut one after the other.)
sentences.i: (These were all the wives Bluebeard had married, and whose throats he had cut, one after another.)
sentences.n: «égorger», from «gorge» ‘throat’, is ‘to cut the throat of’. «C’estoit» stays singular before a plural, as the period allowed; modern French writes «c’étaient». «épousées» and «égorgées» agree with «femmes», which stands before them as the relative «que». The parentheses are the printer’s.

sentences.t: Elle pensa mourir de peur, & la clef du cabinet qu’elle venoit de retirer de la serrure luy tomba de la main :
sentences.say: Elle pensa mourir de peur, et la clef du cabinet qu’elle venait de retirer de la serrure lui tomba de la main :
sentences.l: She came near to dying of fear, and the key of the closet that she had just drawn out of the lock fell from her hand:
sentences.i: She almost died of fright, and the key to the closet, which she had just drawn out of the lock, fell from her hand.
sentences.n: «pensa mourir» is ‘nearly died’, «penser» with an infinitive as on the stairs. «venoit de retirer» is ‘had just drawn out’. «luy tomba de la main» ‘fell to her from the hand’: French names the owner with «luy» and gives the hand «la», where English says ‘her hand’.

sentences.t: aprés avoir un peu repris ses esprits, elle ramassa la clef, referma la porte, & monta à sa chambre pour se remettre un peu, mais elle n’en pouvait venir à bout, tant elle estoit émeuë.
sentences.say: après avoir un peu repris ses esprits, elle ramassa la clef, referma la porte, et monta à sa chambre pour se remettre un peu, mais elle n’en pouvait venir à bout, tant elle était émue.
sentences.l: after having a little recovered her spirits, she picked up the key, shut again the door, and went up to her room to compose herself a little, but she could not come to the end of it, so shaken she was.
sentences.i: When she had somewhat recovered her wits, she picked up the key, shut the door again and went up to her room to collect herself; but she could not manage it, so shaken was she.
sentences.n: «reprendre ses esprits» ‘to take back one’s spirits’ is to come to oneself. «venir à bout de» ‘to come to the end of’ is to manage, to succeed: here she cannot calm herself. «pouvait» is printed with the modern «-ait», beside the «-oit» of «estoit» in the same sentence; the book is not consistent. «émeuë» is «émue» ‘shaken, overcome’.

sentences.t: Ayant remarqué que la clef du cabinet estoit tachée de sang, elle l’essuia deux ou trois fois, mais le sang ne s’en alloit point ;
sentences.say: Ayant remarqué que la clef du cabinet était tachée de sang, elle l’essuya deux ou trois fois, mais le sang ne s’en allait point ;
sentences.l: Having noticed that the key of the closet was stained with blood, she wiped it two or three times, but the blood did not go away at all;
sentences.i: Noticing that the key of the closet was stained with blood, she wiped it two or three times, but the blood would not come off;
sentences.n: «essuia» is the passé simple of «essuyer» ‘to wipe’, printed with «i» for the modern «y». «ne s’en alloit point» ‘did not go away from it at all’: «s’en aller» is ‘to go away’, «alloit» is «allait», and the imperfect says it went on not coming off.

sentences.t: elle eut beau la laver, & mesme la frotter avec du sablon & avec du grais, il y demeura toûjours du sang, car la clef estoit Fée, & il n’y avait pas moyen de la nettoyer tout-à-fait :
sentences.say: elle eut beau la laver, et même la frotter avec du sablon et avec du grès, il y demeura toujours du sang, car la clef était Fée, et il n’y avait pas moyen de la nettoyer tout-à-fait :
sentences.l: in vain she washed it, and even rubbed it with fine sand and with sandstone, there remained always some blood on it, for the key was fairy, and there was no means to clean it entirely:
sentences.i: it was no use washing it, or even scouring it with sand and grit; there was always blood on it, for the key was enchanted, and there was no way to clean it completely:
sentences.n: «Fée» here is an adjective, ‘enchanted, under a fairy’s power’, which is why no scouring will take the blood off the key. Little Thumb uses it of the Ogre’s boots, «comme elles estoient Fées», rendered ‘as they were fairy’ in the literal line and ‘as they were enchanted’ in the idiomatic one. Cinderella’s «Maraine, qui eſtoit Fée» has the same shape but is read as the noun, since the tale goes on to call her «la Fée»: ‘who was a fairy’. «avoir beau» with an infinitive, ‘to have fine (reason) to’, means to do something in vain: «elle eut beau la laver» ‘wash it as she might’. «sablon» is fine sand and «grais» (modern «grès») sandstone, ground for scouring. «mesme» is «même» ‘even’, «toûjours» is «toujours», and «avait» is printed with the modern ending.

sentences.t: quand on ostoit le sang d’un costé, il revenoit de l’autre.
sentences.say: quand on ôtait le sang d’un côté, il revenait de l’autre.
sentences.l: when one took the blood off one side, it came back on the other.
sentences.i: when the blood was taken off one side, it came back on the other.
sentences.n: «ostoit» and «costé» are 1697 spellings of «ôtait» ‘took away’ and «côté» ‘side’. The imperfects say it happened every time she tried.

sentences.t: La Barbe-bleuë revint de son voyage dés le soir mesme, & dit qu’il avoit receu des Lettres dans le chemin, qui luy avoient appris que l’affaire pour laquelle il estoit parti, venoit d’estre terminée à son avantage.
sentences.say: La Barbe-bleue revint de son voyage dès le soir même, et dit qu’il avait reçu des Lettres dans le chemin, qui lui avaient appris que l’affaire pour laquelle il était parti, venait d’être terminée à son avantage.
sentences.l: Blue Beard came back from his journey that very evening, and said that he had received Letters on the road, which had informed him that the business for which he had set out, had just been ended to his advantage.
sentences.i: Bluebeard came home from his journey that same evening, saying he had received letters on the way which told him that the business on which he had set out had just been settled in his favour.
sentences.n: «dés le soir mesme» ‘from the very evening’ is ‘that very evening’. «receu» is «reçu» ‘received’. «apprendre» here is ‘to inform’: the letters «luy avoient appris» ‘had told him’. «venoit d’estre terminée» is ‘had just been concluded’. The witness writes the name here «Barbe-bleuë», with a hyphen; the book spells it several ways.

sentences.t: Sa femme fit tout ce qu’elle put pour lui témoigner qu’elle estoit ravie de son prompt retour.
sentences.say: Sa femme fit tout ce qu’elle put pour lui témoigner qu’elle était ravie de son prompt retour.
sentences.l: His wife did all that she could to show him that she was delighted at his prompt return.
sentences.i: His wife did everything she could to show him how delighted she was that he had come back so soon.
sentences.n: «témoigner» ‘to bear witness’ is here ‘to show’, and «ravie» ‘ravished’ is ‘delighted’. «fit» and «put» are passé simple. «lui» is printed here with the modern i, where the book usually has «luy».

sentences.t: Le lendemain il luy redemanda les clefs, & elle les luy donna, mais d’une main si tremblante, qu’il devina sans peine tout ce qui s’estoit passé.
sentences.say: Le lendemain il lui redemanda les clefs, et elle les lui donna, mais d’une main si tremblante, qu’il devina sans peine tout ce qui s’était passé.
sentences.l: The next day he asked her back for the keys, and she gave them to him, but with a hand so trembling, that he guessed without trouble all that had happened.
sentences.i: The next day he asked her for the keys again, and she gave them to him, but with so unsteady a hand that he easily guessed all that had happened.
sentences.n: «redemander» is ‘to ask for again, ask back’: the prefix «re-» does the work of English ‘back’. In «les luy donna» ‘them to him gave’ both pronouns stand before the verb. «s’estoit passé» ‘had passed itself’ is ‘had happened’, and «devina» is passé simple of «deviner» ‘to guess’.

sentences.t: D’où vient, luy dit-il, que la clef du cabinet n’est point avec les autres : il faut, dit-elle, que je l’aye laissée là haut sur ma table.
sentences.say: D’où vient, lui dit-il, que la clef du cabinet n’est point avec les autres : il faut, dit-elle, que je l’aie laissée là haut sur ma table.
sentences.l: Whence comes it, he said to her, that the key of the closet is not with the others? It must be, she said, that I have left it up there on my table.
sentences.i: How is it, he said, that the key to the closet is not with the others? I must have left it upstairs on my table, she said.
sentences.n: «D’où vient que …» ‘whence comes it that …’ is ‘how is it that …’; the witness closes his question with a colon, and the English gives it a question mark. «il faut que» with the subjunctive («aye», modern «aie») here makes a guess, ‘it must be that’: ‘I must have left it’. «là haut» (modern «là-haut») is ‘up there, upstairs’. «n’est point» is a firm ‘is not’.

sentences.t: Ne manquez pas, dit la Barbe bleuë de me la donner tantost ;
sentences.say: Ne manquez pas, dit la Barbe bleue de me la donner tantôt ;
sentences.l: Do not fail, said Blue Beard, to give it to me presently;
sentences.i: Be sure, said Bluebeard, to let me have it shortly;
sentences.n: «tantost» (modern «tantôt») meant ‘presently, before long’ in 1697; today it is mostly met doubled, ‘now … now’, or in some regions as ‘this afternoon’. «ne manquez pas de» is ‘do not fail to’. The witness has no comma after «Barbe bleuë».

sentences.t: aprés plusieurs remises il falut apporter la clef.
sentences.say: après plusieurs remises il fallut apporter la clef.
sentences.l: after several delays it was needful to bring the key.
sentences.i: after putting it off several times, she had to bring the key.
sentences.n: «remise» here is ‘a putting-off, a delay’. «il falut» (modern «il fallut»), the passé simple of «falloir», is the impersonal ‘it was needful’; English must say who, and the idiomatic line says ‘she had to’.

sentences.t: La Barbe bleuë l’ayant considerée, dit à sa femme, pourquoy y a-t-il du sang sur cette clef ? je n’en sçais rien, répondit la pauvre femme, plus pasle que la mort :
sentences.say: La Barbe bleue l’ayant considérée, dit à sa femme, pourquoi y a-t-il du sang sur cette clef ? je n’en sais rien, répondit la pauvre femme, plus pâle que la mort :
sentences.l: Blue Beard, having looked at it closely, said to his wife, why is there blood on this key? I know nothing of it, answered the poor woman, paler than death:
sentences.i: Bluebeard examined it and said to his wife, Why is there blood on this key? I do not know, answered the poor woman, paler than death.
sentences.n: «considerer» (modern «considérer») is here ‘to look at attentively’, its older, physical sense. «pourquoy y a-t-il» is ‘why is there’, with the 1697 y in «pourquoy». «je n’en sçais rien» ‘I know nothing of it’ has «en» ‘of it’ and «sçais» for «sais». «pasle» is «pâle» ‘pale’.

sentences.t: Vous n’en sçavez rien, reprit la Barbe bleuë, je le sçay bien moy, vous avez voulu entrer dans le cabinet ?
sentences.say: Vous n’en savez rien, reprit la Barbe bleue, je le sais bien moi, vous avez voulu entrer dans le cabinet ?
sentences.l: You know nothing of it, returned Blue Beard, I know it well, I do, you wanted to go into the closet?
sentences.i: You do not know, said Bluebeard, but I know well enough. You wanted to go into the closet, did you?
sentences.n: «reprendre» ‘to take up again’ is ‘to answer back, rejoin’. «je le sçay bien moy» ‘I know it well, me’: the stressed «moy» (modern «moi») sets his knowledge hard against her denial. «sçay» and «sçavez» are 1697 spellings of «sais» and «savez».

sentences.t: Hé bien, Madame, vous y entrerez, & irez prendre vostre place auprés des Dames que vous y avez veuës.
sentences.say: Hé bien, Madame, vous y entrerez, et irez prendre votre place auprès des Dames que vous y avez vues.
sentences.l: Well then, Madame, you will enter there, and will go take your place beside the Ladies that you saw there.
sentences.i: Very well, Madame, you shall go in, and take your place beside the ladies you saw there.
sentences.n: «Hé bien» is «eh bien» ‘well then’. He keeps the courteous «Madame» of a husband of rank even as he pronounces sentence, and his futures «entrerez», «irez» are the sentence. «vostre» is «votre», and «veuës» (modern «vues») agrees with «Dames», which stands before it.

sentences.t: Elle se jetta aux pieds de son Mari, en pleurant & en luy demandant pardon, avec toutes les marques d’un vrai repentir de n’avoir pas esté obeïssante.
sentences.say: Elle se jeta aux pieds de son Mari, en pleurant et en lui demandant pardon, avec toutes les marques d’un vrai repentir de n’avoir pas été obéissante.
sentences.l: She threw herself at the feet of her Husband, weeping and asking him pardon, with all the marks of a true repentance at not having been obedient.
sentences.i: She threw herself at her husband’s feet, weeping and begging his pardon, with every sign of true repentance for having disobeyed him.
sentences.n: «jetta» is the passé simple of «jetter» (modern «jeter») ‘to throw’. «en pleurant & en luy demandant» ‘in weeping and in asking him’ are gerunds, telling how she did it. «marques» are ‘signs’. «obeïssante» (modern «obéissante») has the diaeresis that keeps its «i» a separate vowel.

sentences.t: Elle auroit attendri un rocher, belle & affligée comme elle estoit ;
sentences.say: Elle aurait attendri un rocher, belle et affligée comme elle était ;
sentences.l: She would have softened a rock, beautiful and distressed as she was;
sentences.i: Lovely and stricken as she was, she would have moved a stone to pity;
sentences.n: «auroit attendri» (modern «aurait») is the past conditional, ‘would have softened’; «attendrir» ‘to make tender’ is to move to pity. «affligée» ‘afflicted’ is ‘grief-stricken, in distress’.

sentences.t: mais la Barbe bleuë avoit un cœur plus dur qu’un rocher :
sentences.say: mais la Barbe bleue avait un cœur plus dur qu’un rocher :
sentences.l: but Blue Beard had a heart harder than a rock:
sentences.i: but Bluebeard had a heart harder than stone.
sentences.n: The rock comes back at once: she might have softened «un rocher», but his heart is harder than one. «cœur» is ‘heart’, and «avoit» the imperfect of a lasting state.

sentences.t: Il faut mourir, Madame, luy dit-il, & toute à l’heure.
sentences.say: Il faut mourir, Madame, lui dit-il, et toute à l’heure.
sentences.l: It is needful to die, Madame, he said to her, and this very moment.
sentences.i: You must die, Madame, he said, and at once.
sentences.n: «il faut mourir» ‘it is needful to die’ is impersonal: French need not say who must die, and English must. «toute à l’heure» (modern «tout à l’heure») meant ‘this very moment, at once’ in 1697; today it means ‘in a little while’ or ‘a little while ago’.

sentences.t: Puis qu’il faut mourir, répondit elle, en le regardant les yeux baignez de larmes, donnez moy un peu de tems pour prier Dieu.
sentences.say: Puis qu’il faut mourir, répondit elle, en le regardant les yeux baignez de larmes, donnez moi un peu de temps pour prier Dieu.
sentences.l: Since it is needful to die, she answered, looking at him, the eyes bathed in tears, give me a little time to pray to God.
sentences.i: Since I must die, she answered, looking at him with her eyes full of tears, give me a little time to pray to God.
sentences.n: «Puis que» is «puisque» ‘since’, and she takes up his impersonal «il faut mourir». «les yeux baignez de larmes» ‘the eyes bathed in tears’ describes her without a verb, where English says ‘with her eyes’; «baignez» is «baignés». «tems» is an older spelling of «temps» ‘time’, and «moy» is «moi». She still says «vous» to him («donnez»).

sentences.t: Je vous donne un demy-quart-heure, reprit la Barbe bleuë, mais pas un moment davantage.
sentences.say: Je vous donne un demi-quart-heure, reprit la Barbe bleue, mais pas un moment davantage.
sentences.l: I give you a half-quarter-hour, returned Blue Beard, but not one moment more.
sentences.i: I give you half a quarter of an hour, said Bluebeard, and not a moment longer.
sentences.n: A «demy-quart-heure» (modern «demi-quart d’heure») is half of a quarter of an hour: seven and a half minutes. «demy» is «demi», with the 1697 y, and «davantage» is ‘more’.

sentences.t: Lors qu’elle fut seule, elle appella sa sœur, & luy dit, ma sœur Anne, car elle s’appelloit ainsi, monte je te prie sur le haut de la Tour, pour voir si mes freres ne viennent point, ils m’ont promis qu’ils me viendroient voir aujourd’huy, & si tu les vois, fais-leur signe de se hâter.
sentences.say: Lors qu’elle fut seule, elle appela sa sœur, et lui dit, ma sœur Anne, car elle s’appelait ainsi, monte je te prie sur le haut de la Tour, pour voir si mes frères ne viennent point, ils m’ont promis qu’ils me viendraient voir aujourd’huy, et si tu les vois, fais-leur signe de se hâter.
sentences.l: When she was alone, she called her sister, and said to her, my sister Anne, for she was called so, go up I pray you onto the top of the Tower, to see if my brothers are not coming, they have promised me that they would come see me today, and if you see them, make them a sign to hurry.
sentences.i: When she was alone she called her sister and said to her, My sister Anne (for that was her name), go up, I beg you, to the top of the tower and see whether my brothers are coming; they promised me they would come to see me today, and if you see them, signal to them to make haste.
sentences.n: «Lors qu’elle fut seule» is «lorsqu’elle fut seule» ‘when she was alone’, with «fut» in the passé simple. «car elle s’appelloit ainsi» ‘for she called herself so’ is ‘for that was her name’; «appella» and «appelloit» double the l of modern «appela», «appelait». The wife says «tu» to her sister («monte», «si tu les vois», «fais»), the address of intimacy, and «je te prie» is ‘I beg you’. «si mes freres ne viennent point» ‘whether my brothers are not coming’ hopes for a yes. «me viendroient voir» sets «me» before «viendroient», where modern French says «viendraient me voir». «faire signe» ‘to make a sign’ is to signal, and «aujourd’huy» is «aujourd’hui».

sentences.t: La sœur Anne monta sur le haut de la Tour,
sentences.l: Sister Anne went up onto the top of the Tower,
sentences.i: Sister Anne climbed to the top of the tower,
sentences.n: «monta» is the passé simple of «monter» ‘to go up’. «la sœur Anne» ‘the sister Anne’ is simply ‘Sister Anne’ in English.

sentences.t: & la pauvre affligée luy crioit de temps en temps, Anne, ma sœur Anne, ne vois-tu rien venir.
sentences.say: et la pauvre affligée lui criait de temps en temps, Anne, ma sœur Anne, ne vois-tu rien venir.
sentences.l: and the poor afflicted one cried to her from time to time, Anne, my sister Anne, see you nothing coming?
sentences.i: and every so often the poor distressed wife would call up to her, Anne, my sister Anne, do you see nothing coming?
sentences.n: «ne … rien» is ‘nothing’ and «voir venir» is ‘to see (something) coming’. The witness prints the call four times, never with a question mark, as «vois-tu», «vois tu» and once «voy tu», an older spelling of the same «vois»; Lectorium prints each as it stands, and the English gives the same words, with a question mark, every time. The wife says «tu» to her sister and «vous» to her husband; all of it is ‘you’ in the English. «la pauvre affligée» ‘the poor afflicted (woman)’ uses the adjective as a noun. «crioit» (modern «criait») is imperfect, so she called again and again, and «crier» here is ‘to call out’, not ‘to weep’.

sentences.t: Et la sœur Anne luy répondoit, je ne vois rien que le soleil qui poudroye, et l’herbe qui verdoye.
sentences.say: Et la sœur Anne lui répondait, je ne vois rien que le soleil qui poudroie, et l’herbe qui verdoie.
sentences.l: And Sister Anne answered her, I see nothing but the sun that makes the dust shine, and the grass that grows green.
sentences.i: And Sister Anne would answer, I see nothing but the sunlight glinting on the dust, and the grass growing green.
sentences.n: «ne … rien que» is ‘nothing but’. «poudroye» and «verdoye» (1697 spellings of «poudroie», «verdoie») are verbs built on «poudre» ‘dust’ and «vert» ‘green’: the sun lights up the dust in the air, though the French leaves open whether it raises the dust or only shines through it, and the grass shows green. The two verbs rhyme in the French and the English does not. When the answer comes a second time the witness prints «Soleil» with a capital and no comma before «et». «répondoit», an imperfect like «crioit», is an answer given each time she is asked.

sentences.t: Cependant la Barbe bleüe tenant un grand coutelas à sa main, crioit de toute sa force à sa femme, descens viste, où je monteray là-haut.
sentences.say: Cependant la Barbe bleue tenant un grand coutelas à sa main, criait de toute sa force à sa femme, descends vite, où je monterai là-haut.
sentences.l: Meanwhile Blue Beard, holding a great cutlass in his hand, cried with all his strength to his wife, come down quick, or I will go up there.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Bluebeard, a great cutlass in his hand, was shouting to his wife at the top of his voice, Come down at once, or I shall come up.
sentences.n: «Cependant» is ‘meanwhile’. A «coutelas» is a cutlass, a short, broad sword with a single cutting edge. «descens» (modern «descends») is a «tu» form: until now he has spoken to his wife with «vous», and now he shouts at her with the «tu» of anger and command, while she goes on saying «vous» to him. The English stays ‘you’. «viste» is «vite» ‘quickly’, and «monteray» is «monterai» ‘I will go up’. The witness prints «où» ‘where’; the sense requires «ou» ‘or’, here and again below, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Encore un moment s’il vous plait, luy répondit sa femme, & aussi-tost elle crioit tout bas.
sentences.say: Encore un moment s’il vous plaît, lui répondit sa femme, et aussitôt elle criait tout bas.
sentences.l: Yet one moment if you please, his wife answered him, and at once she cried very low.
sentences.i: One moment more, if you please, his wife answered, and at once she called out under her breath:
sentences.n: «Encore un moment» ‘still one moment’ is ‘one moment more’, and she still says «vous» («s’il vous plait», modern «plaît»). «crioit tout bas» ‘cried quite low’: she calls to her sister in a low voice. The witness puts a full stop after «bas», though the call follows at once.

sentences.t: Anne, ma sœur Anne, ne vois tu rien venir,
sentences.l: Anne, my sister Anne, see you nothing coming?
sentences.i: Anne, my sister Anne, do you see nothing coming?
sentences.n: «ne … rien» is ‘nothing’ and «voir venir» is ‘to see (something) coming’. The witness prints the call four times, never with a question mark, as «vois-tu», «vois tu» and once «voy tu», an older spelling of the same «vois»; Lectorium prints each as it stands, and the English gives the same words, with a question mark, every time. The wife says «tu» to her sister and «vous» to her husband; all of it is ‘you’ in the English. Here the witness prints «vois tu» without its hyphen, and ends the call with a comma.

sentences.t: & la sœur Anne, répondoit, je ne vois rien que le Soleil qui poudroye et l’herbe qui verdoye.
sentences.say: et la sœur Anne, répondait, je ne vois rien que le Soleil qui poudroie et l’herbe qui verdoie.
sentences.l: and Sister Anne answered, I see nothing but the sun that makes the dust shine, and the grass that grows green.
sentences.i: and Sister Anne would answer, I see nothing but the sunlight glinting on the dust, and the grass growing green.
sentences.n: «ne … rien que» is ‘nothing but’. «poudroye» and «verdoye» (1697 spellings of «poudroie», «verdoie») are verbs built on «poudre» ‘dust’ and «vert» ‘green’: the sun lights up the dust in the air, though the French leaves open whether it raises the dust or only shines through it, and the grass shows green. The two verbs rhyme in the French and the English does not. When the answer comes a second time the witness prints «Soleil» with a capital and no comma before «et». The witness also sets a comma between «la sœur Anne» and her verb «répondoit».

sentences.t: Descens donc viste, crioit la Barbe bleuë, où je monteray la haut.
sentences.say: Descends donc vite, criait la Barbe bleue, où je monterai la haut.
sentences.l: Come down then quick, cried Blue Beard, or I will go up there.
sentences.i: Come down, then, and quickly, shouted Bluebeard, or I shall come up.
sentences.n: «donc» ‘then’ presses the order, still in the «tu» form «descens». As before, the witness prints «où» where the sense requires «ou» ‘or’, and «la haut» without the accent of «là-haut» ‘up there’; Lectorium prints both as they stand.

sentences.t: Je m’en vais, répondoit sa femme,
sentences.say: Je m’en vais, répondait sa femme,
sentences.l: I am going, his wife answered,
sentences.i: I am coming, his wife would answer,
sentences.n: «Je m’en vais» ‘I am going away’ is said here as ‘I am on my way’, a promise to come down. «répondoit» is imperfect, one answer in a repeated exchange.

sentences.t: & puis elle crioit Anne, ma sœur Anne, ne voy tu rien venir.
sentences.say: et puis elle criait Anne, ma sœur Anne, ne vois tu rien venir.
sentences.l: and then she cried, Anne, my sister Anne, see you nothing coming?
sentences.i: and then she would call, Anne, my sister Anne, do you see nothing coming?
sentences.n: «ne … rien» is ‘nothing’ and «voir venir» is ‘to see (something) coming’. The witness prints the call four times, never with a question mark, as «vois-tu», «vois tu» and once «voy tu», an older spelling of the same «vois»; Lectorium prints each as it stands, and the English gives the same words, with a question mark, every time. The wife says «tu» to her sister and «vous» to her husband; all of it is ‘you’ in the English. This time the witness prints «voy tu», and no comma after «crioit».

sentences.t: Je vois, répondit la sœur Anne, une grosse poussiere qui vient de ce costé-cy.
sentences.say: Je vois, répondit la sœur Anne, une grosse poussière qui vient de ce côté-ci.
sentences.l: I see, answered Sister Anne, a great dust that is coming from this side here.
sentences.i: I see, answered Sister Anne, a great cloud of dust coming this way.
sentences.n: The answer changes, and the tense with it: «répondit» is passé simple, a single answer, where «répondoit» was an answer repeated. «une grosse poussiere» ‘a big dust’ is a cloud of dust, and «poussiere» lacks the accent of «poussière». «de ce costé-cy» (modern «de ce côté-ci») ‘from this side here’ is ‘this way’.

sentences.t: Sont-ce mes freres ? Helas, non, ma sœur, c’est un Troupeau de Moutons.
sentences.say: Sont-ce mes frères ? Hélas, non, ma sœur, c’est un Troupeau de Moutons.
sentences.l: Are they my brothers? Alas, no, my sister, it is a Flock of Sheep.
sentences.i: Is it my brothers? Alas, no, sister, it is a flock of sheep.
sentences.n: The wife asks and Anne answers, with no tags to say who is speaking. «Sont-ce» ‘are they’ inverts «ce sont». «freres» and «Helas» lack the accents of «frères» and «hélas», and the capitals on «Troupeau» and «Moutons» are the printer’s.

sentences.t: Ne veus tu pas descendre, crioit la Barbe bleuë.
sentences.say: Ne veux tu pas descendre, criait la Barbe bleue.
sentences.l: Do you not want to come down? cried Blue Beard.
sentences.i: Will you not come down? shouted Bluebeard.
sentences.n: «veus» is an old spelling of «veux», the «tu» form of «vouloir» ‘to want’: ‘do you not want to’, which English hears as ‘will you not’. The witness ends the question with a full stop.

sentences.t: Encore un moment répondoit sa femme,
sentences.say: Encore un moment répondait sa femme,
sentences.l: Yet one moment, answered his wife,
sentences.i: One moment more, his wife would answer,
sentences.n: The same plea as before, now in the imperfect «répondoit», one answer among many.

sentences.t: & puis elle crioit, Anne, ma sœur Anne, ne vois tu rien venir.
sentences.say: et puis elle criait, Anne, ma sœur Anne, ne vois tu rien venir.
sentences.l: and then she cried, Anne, my sister Anne, see you nothing coming?
sentences.i: and then she would call, Anne, my sister Anne, do you see nothing coming?
sentences.n: «ne … rien» is ‘nothing’ and «voir venir» is ‘to see (something) coming’. The witness prints the call four times, never with a question mark, as «vois-tu», «vois tu» and once «voy tu», an older spelling of the same «vois»; Lectorium prints each as it stands, and the English gives the same words, with a question mark, every time. The wife says «tu» to her sister and «vous» to her husband; all of it is ‘you’ in the English. This is the fourth and last time she calls.

sentences.t: Je vois, répondit-elle, deux Cavaliers qui viennent de ce costé-cy, mais ils sont bien loin encore :
sentences.say: Je vois, répondit-elle, deux Cavaliers qui viennent de ce côté-ci, mais ils sont bien loin encore :
sentences.l: I see, she answered, two Horsemen who are coming from this side here, but they are very far still:
sentences.i: I see, she answered, two horsemen coming this way, but they are still a long way off.
sentences.n: «Cavaliers» here are ‘horsemen, riders’, the plain sense of the word. «bien loin» ‘well far’ is ‘a long way off’, with «bien» strengthening, as it often does.

sentences.t: Dieu soit loué, s’ecria-t-elle un moment aprés, ce sont mes freres ; je leur fais signe tant que je puis de se haster.
sentences.say: Dieu soit loué, s’écria-t-elle un moment après, ce sont mes frères ; je leur fais signe tant que je puis de se hâter.
sentences.l: God be praised, she exclaimed a moment after, it is my brothers; I am making them a sign as much as I can to hurry.
sentences.i: God be praised, she cried a moment later, it is my brothers! I am signalling to them as hard as I can to make haste.
sentences.n: Anne is still the speaker. «Dieu soit loué» ‘God be praised’ is a wish in the subjunctive. The «-t-» of «s’ecria-t-elle» (modern «s’écria») is put in only for the sound, between two vowels. «tant que je puis» ‘as much as I can’ uses «puis», a first-person form of «pouvoir» that modern French keeps only in formal use, beside everyday «peux». «haster» is «hâter»: the book prints both spellings within this one tale.

sentences.t: La Barbe bleüe se mit à crier si fort que toute la maison en trembla.
sentences.say: La Barbe bleue se mit à crier si fort que toute la maison en trembla.
sentences.l: Blue Beard set himself to shout so loud that the whole house trembled from it.
sentences.i: Bluebeard began to shout so loudly that the whole house shook.
sentences.n: «se mettre à» ‘to put oneself to’ is ‘to begin to’. «en» in «en trembla» is ‘from it’, the shouting.

sentences.t: La pauvre femme descendit, & alla se jetter à ses pieds toute épleurée & toute échevelée :
sentences.say: La pauvre femme descendit, et alla se jeter à ses pieds toute éplorée et toute échevelée :
sentences.l: The poor woman came down, and went to throw herself at his feet all in tears and all dishevelled:
sentences.i: The poor woman came down and threw herself at his feet, all in tears, her hair in disorder.
sentences.n: «épleurée» (modern «éplorée») is ‘in tears’, and «échevelée», from «cheveux» ‘hair’, is ‘with her hair loose and disordered’. «toute» agrees with «femme», ‘wholly’. «alla se jetter» is ‘went to throw herself’.

sentences.t: cela ne sert de rien, dit la Barbe bleuë, il faut mourir ;
sentences.say: cela ne sert de rien, dit la Barbe bleue, il faut mourir ;
sentences.l: that serves for nothing, said Blue Beard, it is needful to die;
sentences.i: That will do no good, said Bluebeard; you must die.
sentences.n: «ne sert de rien» ‘serves for nothing’ is ‘is of no use’. «il faut mourir» comes once more, the impersonal sentence of death.

sentences.t: puis la prenant d’une main par les cheveux, & de l’autre levant le coutelas en l’air, il alloit luy abattre la teste.
sentences.say: puis la prenant d’une main par les cheveux, et de l’autre levant le coutelas en l’air, il allait lui abattre la tête.
sentences.l: then taking her with one hand by the hair, and with the other raising the cutlass in the air, he was going to strike off her head.
sentences.i: then, seizing her by the hair with one hand and raising the cutlass high with the other, he was about to strike off her head.
sentences.n: «il alloit» (modern «allait») with an infinitive is ‘he was about to’, the act caught just before it happens. «abattre» is ‘to strike down, cut off’, and «luy … la teste» ‘to her the head’ is ‘her head’. «prenant» and «levant» are present participles.

sentences.t: La pauvre femme se tournant vers luy, & le regardant avec des yeux mourans, le pria de luy donner un petit moment pour se recueillir :
sentences.say: La pauvre femme se tournant vers lui, et le regardant avec des yeux mourants, le pria de lui donner un petit moment pour se recueillir :
sentences.l: The poor woman, turning toward him, and looking at him with dying eyes, begged him to give her a little moment to recollect herself:
sentences.i: The poor woman turned towards him and, looking at him with dying eyes, begged him to give her one short moment to collect herself.
sentences.n: «se recueillir» ‘to gather oneself in’ is to collect one’s thoughts, especially for prayer. «yeux mourans» (modern «mourants») are ‘dying eyes’, eyes that seem to be failing. «pria» is the passé simple of «prier», which is both ‘to beg’ and ‘to pray’.

sentences.t: Non, non, dit-il, & recommande-toy bien à Dieu ; & levant son bras…
sentences.say: Non, non, dit-il, et recommande-toi bien à Dieu ; et levant son bras…
sentences.l: No, no, he said, and commend yourself well to God; and raising his arm…
sentences.i: No, no, he said, commend your soul to God; and, raising his arm…
sentences.n: «se recommander à Dieu» ‘to commend oneself to God’ is to pray for one’s soul before death. «recommande-toy» (modern «recommande-toi») is the «tu» form again; the English stays ‘you’. The sentence breaks off at «bras» with the printer’s dots.

sentences.t: Dans ce moment on heurta si fort à la porte, que la Barbe bleuë s’arresta tout court :
sentences.say: Dans ce moment on heurta si fort à la porte, que la Barbe bleue s’arrêta tout court :
sentences.l: In that moment one knocked so hard at the door, that Blue Beard stopped quite short:
sentences.i: At that moment there came such a knocking at the door that Bluebeard stopped dead.
sentences.n: «heurter à la porte» ‘to strike at the door’ is to knock, here loudly; «on» ‘one’ is ‘someone’. «s’arresta tout court» (modern «s’arrêta») is ‘stopped himself quite short’.

sentences.t: on ouvrit, et aussi-tost on vit entrer deux Cavaliers, qui mettant l’épée à la main, coururent droit à la Barbe bleüe.
sentences.say: on ouvrit, et aussitôt on vit entrer deux Cavaliers, qui mettant l’épée à la main, coururent droit à la Barbe bleue.
sentences.l: one opened, and at once one saw enter two Horsemen, who putting sword in hand, ran straight at Blue Beard.
sentences.i: The door was opened, and in at once came two horsemen, who drew their swords and ran straight at Bluebeard.
sentences.n: «on ouvrit … on vit» ‘one opened … one saw’: French leaves the doer unnamed, and English turns to the passive. «mettre l’épée à la main» ‘to put the sword in the hand’ is to draw. «coururent» is the passé simple of «courir» ‘to run’.

sentences.t: Il reconnut que c’étoit les freres de sa femme, l’un Dragon & l’autre Mousquetaire, desorte qu’il s’enfuit aussi-tost pour se sauver ;
sentences.say: Il reconnut que c’était les frères de sa femme, l’un Dragon et l’autre Mousquetaire, desorte qu’il s’enfuit aussitôt pour se sauver ;
sentences.l: He recognised that it was the brothers of his wife, the one a Dragoon and the other a Musketeer, so that he fled at once to save himself;
sentences.i: He saw that they were his wife’s brothers, one a dragoon and the other a musketeer, and at once he fled to save himself;
sentences.n: A «Dragon» was a dragoon, a soldier who rode to battle and could fight on foot; a «Mousquetaire» was one of the King’s Musketeers, the mounted guard of the royal household, whose ranks were filled with young gentlemen. «c’étoit» is printed with the accent of modern «c’était» but the old «-oit», and singular before a plural, as «C’estoit» was earlier. «desorte que» is «de sorte que» ‘so that’, printed as one word. «s’enfuit» is now the passé simple ‘fled’.

sentences.t: mais les deux freres le poursuivirent desi prés, qu’ils l’attraperent avant qu’il pust gagner le perron :
sentences.say: mais les deux frères le poursuivirent desi près, qu’ils l’attrapèrent avant qu’il pût gagner le perron :
sentences.l: but the two brothers pursued him so closely, that they caught him before he could reach the front steps:
sentences.i: but the two brothers pursued him so hard that they caught him before he could reach the steps at the door.
sentences.n: «desi prés» is «de si près» ‘so closely’, printed as one word, like «desorte» just before; Lectorium prints it as it stands. The «perron» is the flight of stone steps outside the entrance of a great house. «pust» (modern «pût») is the imperfect subjunctive that «avant que» ‘before’ calls for, and «poursuivirent», «attraperent» are passé simple.

sentences.t: Ils luy passerent leur épée au travers du corps, & le laisserent mort.
sentences.say: Ils lui passèrent leur épée au travers du corps, et le laissèrent mort.
sentences.l: They passed their sword through his body, and left him dead.
sentences.i: They ran him through with their swords and left him dead.
sentences.n: «passer l’épée au travers du corps» ‘to pass the sword through the body’ is to run someone through, and «luy» ‘to him’ says whose body. «leur épée» is singular because each brother has one sword; English makes it plural in the idiomatic line.

sentences.t: La pauvre femme estoit presque aussi morte que son Mari, & n’avoit pas la force de se lever pour embrasser ses freres.
sentences.say: La pauvre femme était presque aussi morte que son Mari, et n’avait pas la force de se lever pour embrasser ses frères.
sentences.l: The poor woman was almost as dead as her Husband, and had not the strength to rise to embrace her brothers.
sentences.i: The poor woman was almost as dead as her husband, and had not the strength to rise and embrace her brothers.
sentences.n: «presque aussi morte que son Mari» ‘almost as dead as her husband’ is the narrator’s own comparison, as dry as it sounds. «embrasser» is ‘to take in one’s arms’, as when her husband left.

sentences.t: Il se trouva que la Barbe bleüe n’avoit point d’heritiers, & qu’ainsi sa femme demeura maîtresse de tous ses biens.
sentences.say: Il se trouva que la Barbe bleue n’avait point d’héritiers, et qu’ainsi sa femme demeura maîtresse de tous ses biens.
sentences.l: It turned out that Blue Beard had no heirs, and that thus his wife remained mistress of all his goods.
sentences.i: It turned out that Bluebeard had no heirs, and so his wife was left mistress of all his wealth.
sentences.n: «Il se trouva que» ‘it found itself that’ is ‘it turned out that’. «biens» ‘goods’ is property of every kind, land and money alike. «maîtresse» has the circumflex of modern spelling, where the tale elsewhere writes «Maistre», and «heritiers» lacks the accent of «héritiers».

sentences.t: Elle en employa une partie à marier sa sœur Anne avec un jeune Gentilhomme, dont elle estoit aimée depuis long-temps ;
sentences.say: Elle en employa une partie à marier sa sœur Anne avec un jeune Gentilhomme, dont elle était aimée depuis longtemps ;
sentences.l: She used a part of it to marry her sister Anne to a young Gentleman, by whom she had been loved a long time;
sentences.i: She spent part of it on marrying her sister Anne to a young gentleman who had long loved her;
sentences.n: «en» ‘of it’ is the fortune, and «employa» is passé simple. «marier» ‘to marry off’ is to give in marriage, which meant providing a dowry. A «Gentilhomme» was a man of noble birth. «dont elle estoit aimée depuis long-temps» ‘by whom she was loved since long’: French uses the imperfect with «depuis» where English says ‘had long been loved’.

sentences.t: une autre partie à acheter des Charges de Capitaine à ses deux freres ; & le reste à se marier elle-mesme à un fort honneste homme, qui luy fit oublier le mauvais temps qu’elle avoit passé avec la Barbe bleuë.
sentences.say: une autre partie à acheter des Charges de Capitaine à ses deux frères ; et le reste à se marier elle-même à un fort honnête homme, qui lui fit oublier le mauvais temps qu’elle avait passé avec la Barbe bleue.
sentences.l: another part to buy Commissions of Captain for her two brothers; and the rest to marry herself to a very worthy man, who made her forget the bad time that she had spent with Blue Beard.
sentences.i: another part on buying captains’ commissions for her two brothers; and the rest on her own marriage to a true gentleman, who made her forget the wretched time she had spent with Bluebeard.
sentences.n: A «Charge» was a post that was bought and owned: in Perrault’s France a man paid for a captain’s commission, and with it the command of a company. «un fort honneste homme» ‘a very worthy man’ repeats word for word what the younger sister once thought of Bluebeard at the country house, now said of her second husband. «elle-mesme» is «elle-même» ‘herself’, and «fit oublier» is ‘made forget’.

sentences.t: MORALITÉ.
sentences.l: MORAL
sentences.n: «Moralité» is ‘moral’, the lesson drawn from a story. Each tale in the book ends with one in verse, and several with two, as the title page promises («Avec des Moralitez»). They are worldly, witty lines addressed to polite society, and they do not always agree with the tale they follow, or with each other.

sentences.t:
LA curiosité, malgré tous ses attraits,
Couste souvent bien des regrets ;
sentences.say:
LA curiosité, malgré tous ses attraits,
Coûte souvent bien des regrets ;
sentences.l:
Curiosity, in spite of all its charms,
Costs often a good many regrets;
sentences.i:
Curiosity, for all its charms,
Often costs a great deal of regret;
sentences.n: «LA» in capitals is the printer’s way of opening the verse. «attraits» are ‘attractions, charms’. «Couste» is the 1697 spelling of «coûte» ‘costs’. «bien des regrets» ‘well of regrets’ is ‘many regrets’: «bien des» means ‘many’. The moral is in rhymed lines of different lengths, and the English follows it line for line without rhyme.

sentences.t:
On en voit, tous les jours, mille exemples paroistre,
C’est, n’endeplaise au sexe, un plaisir bien leger,
Dés qu’on le prend, il cesse d’estre,
Et toûjours il couste trop cher.
sentences.say:
On en voit, tous les jours, mille exemples paraître,
C’est, n’endeplaise au sexe, un plaisir bien léger,
Dès qu’on le prend, il cesse d’être,
Et toujours il coûte trop cher.
sentences.l:
One sees of it, every day, a thousand examples appear,
It is, may it not displease the sex, a pleasure very slight,
As soon as one takes it, it ceases to be,
And always it costs too dear.
sentences.i:
Every day a thousand instances of it come to light;
It is, with all respect to the ladies, a slight pleasure:
The moment one takes it, it is gone,
And it always costs too much.
sentences.n: «On en voit … mille exemples paroistre» is ‘one sees a thousand examples of it appear’: «en» is ‘of it’, curiosity, and «paroistre» is «paraître». «n’en déplaise à» ‘may it not displease’ is ‘with all respect to, begging the pardon of’; the witness prints «n’endeplaise» as a single word, and Lectorium prints it unaltered. «le sexe» used on its own meant ‘women’ in the 17th century, so the aside lays curiosity at women’s door with a mock bow. «leger» is «léger» ‘light, slight’. In the last two lines «il» is the pleasure; «Dés», «estre» and «toûjours» are «dès», «être» and «toujours».

sentences.t: AUTRE MORALITÉ.
sentences.l: ANOTHER MORAL
sentences.n: «Autre» is ‘other, another’: a second moral, lighter than the first.

sentences.t:
POur peu qu’on ait l’esprit sensé,
Et que du monde on sçache le grimoire,
On voit bien-tost que cette histoire
Est un conte du temps passé ;
sentences.say:
POur peu qu’on ait l’esprit sensé,
Et que du monde on sache le grimoire,
On voit bientôt que cette histoire,
Est un conte du temps passé ;
sentences.l:
If one has in the least a sensible mind,
And of the world may know the book of spells,
One sees soon that this story
Is a tale of times past;
sentences.i:
Anyone with a grain of sense
Who knows the hidden ways of the world
Sees soon enough that this story
Is a tale of times past;
sentences.n: «POur» in capitals is again the printer’s opening. «pour peu que» ‘for however little that’ takes the subjunctive («ait», «sçache»): ‘if one has even a little’. A «grimoire» is a magician’s book of spells, and so anything obscure and hard to read: to know the «grimoire» of the world is to know its secret workings. «bien-tost» is «bientôt» ‘soon’. «un conte du temps passé» takes up the book’s own title, «Histoires ou contes du temps passé»: the moral declares the story itself old-fashioned.

sentences.t:
Il n’est plus d’Epoux si terrible,
Ny qui demande l’impossible,
Fut-il mal-content & jaloux,
Prés de sa femme on le voit filer doux ;
sentences.say:
Il n’est plus d’Époux si terrible,
Ni qui demande l’impossible,
Fut-il mal-content et jaloux,
Près de sa femme on le voit filer doux ;
sentences.l:
There is no longer a husband so terrible,
Nor one who demands the impossible,
Were he discontented and jealous,
Near his wife one sees him spin soft;
sentences.i:
No husband now is so fearsome,
Or asks for what cannot be done,
Though he be sullen and jealous,
At his wife’s side he is all meekness;
sentences.n: «Il n’est plus de» ‘there is no more any’ is the literary «être» for ‘there is’, and «Ny» is «ni» ‘nor’. «Epoux» ‘husband’ lacks its modern accent («époux»). «Fut-il» ‘were he’ puts the verb first to concede: it stands for «fût-il», the imperfect subjunctive printed without its circumflex. «mal-content» (modern «mécontent») is ‘discontented, surly’. «filer doux» ‘to spin soft’ is to behave meekly and give no trouble; what picture lies behind the idiom, soft spinning or a rope paid out gently, is not certain. «Prés» is «près» ‘near’.

sentences.t:
Et de quelque couleur que sa barbe puisse estre,
On a peine à juger qui des deux est le maistre.
sentences.say:
Et de quelque couleur que sa barbe puisse être,
On a peine à juger qui des deux est le maître.
sentences.l:
And of whatever colour his beard may be,
One has trouble judging which of the two is the master.
sentences.i:
And whatever the colour of his beard,
It is hard to tell which of the two is master.
sentences.n: «de quelque couleur que» with the subjunctive «puisse» is ‘of whatever colour’. «sa barbe» is ‘his beard’, «sa» agreeing with «barbe». «avoir peine à» ‘to have pain at’ is ‘to find it hard to’. «maistre» is «maître» ‘master’: in marriages of the present day, the moral teases, it is hard to say who rules.
